theme: Godliness; widows and elders; the good fight
readingInstruction: Read 1 Timothy 4:1-6:21. Paul gives Timothy instruction on guarding against false teaching, on his own example and ministry, on caring for various groups in the church, and on the dangers of money. Notice how often Paul turns from doctrine to daily conduct.
settingTheScene: Paul continues his letter to Timothy in Ephesus. False teachers were forbidding marriage and certain foods, and others were using religion for profit. Timothy was young and perhaps timid. Paul encourages him to be an example, to devote himself to public reading of Scripture, and to fight the good fight of faith. The letter also gives guidance for widows, elders, slaves and masters, and the rich.
observation: “For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (4:4).
“For while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way” (4:8).
“Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity” (4:12).
“Devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching” (4:13).
“Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in this, for by so doing you will save both yourself and your hearers” (4:16).
“But godliness with contentment is great gain” (6:6).
“For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils” (6:10).
“Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called” (6:12).
interpretation:
Chapter 4 opens with a warning that in later times some will depart from the faith, devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons. They forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods. Paul answers with creation: “For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer.” Marriage and food are gifts. Christians are free to enjoy them with gratitude, though not to worship them.

Timothy is to be a good servant of Christ Jesus, nourished on the words of the faith. He is to have nothing to do with irreverent myths and to train himself for godliness. “For while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way, as it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come.” Exercise is good, but spiritual discipline matters more and lasts. “Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.” Authority comes from example. Until Paul arrives, Timothy is to give attention to Scripture reading, exhortation, and teaching, and not to neglect the gift given to him when the elders laid their hands on him. “Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching.” A pastor must watch both his life and his doctrine.

Chapter 5 gives practical guidance. Treat older men as fathers, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity. Care for widows who are truly in need, and let families care for their own: “If anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.” Elders who rule well are worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching, and the worker deserves his wages. Accusations against an elder require two or three witnesses, and those who persist in sin are to be rebuked publicly. Timothy is to keep these rules without prejudice or partiality, to be careful about laying on hands hastily, and to keep himself pure. Paul adds a small word about his health: “No longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments.”

Chapter 6 speaks to slaves and masters, and to false teachers who suppose that godliness is a means of gain. “But godliness with contentment is great gain, for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world.” Those who desire to be rich fall into temptation. “For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pangs.” Note that it is the love of money, not money itself. Timothy is to flee these things and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness. “Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called.” The rich are to be generous and rich in good works, storing up treasure as a good foundation for the future. The letter ends with a plea: “O Timothy, guard the deposit entrusted to you.”
connection: Genesis 1:31 and Mark 7:19 affirm the goodness of creation and food. Hebrews 13:4 honors marriage. Acts 16:1-3 introduces Timothy. 2 Timothy 1:6 mentions his gift. Deuteronomy 25:4 and Luke 10:7 are behind the wage principle. Philippians 4:11-13 speaks of contentment. Matthew 6:19-24 teaches that we cannot serve God and money. Hebrews 13:5 says to be content with what you have. Ecclesiastes 5:10 warns about loving money. Jude 3 speaks of contending for the faith.
application:
Receive your next meal and a gift in your life with thanksgiving, and say the prayer aloud.

Ask which area of your life (speech, conduct, love, faith, purity) most needs to be an example, and take one step.

Examine your relationship with money. Ask: what do I love? Plan one generous gift this week.
prayerPrompts: Receive God’s gifts with thanksgiving, and name some.
Ask him to train you for godliness.
Ask him to help you fight the good fight of faith.
